name: News Feed
tagline: Grow a social feed from one SQL query to precomputed timelines, ranking and global media
summary: A news feed shows each user the recent posts of the people they follow. At 10,000 users it is one SQL query. At 100 million it is the canonical hard problem of read-heavy social systems: a post by one account must reach millions of followers within seconds, feed loads must stay fast no matter how many accounts a user follows, and the product eventually wants ranking instead of chronology. Each step keeps the previous design and adds only what the new bottleneck demands, with the write-time versus read-time fan-out trade-off at the centre.
requirements: Users publish posts (text plus optional images or video) and follow other users.
Opening the feed returns the most recent posts from followed users in well under 200 ms at p99.
A new post is visible to followers within a few seconds of being published.
A user may follow thousands of accounts; some accounts have tens of millions of followers.
The feed can be ranked by relevance (recency plus engagement) rather than strictly by time.
Reads outnumber writes by roughly 100:1 and the service stays available when a dependency degrades.
Images and video load quickly for users on every continent.

steps.title: Pull model: one query at read time
steps.problem: Nothing has broken yet — this is the starting point. The requirement is simply 'show me recent posts from people I follow', and the smallest system that meets it is a relational schema with two tables and one query.
steps.why: Fan-out on read, also called the pull model: when a user opens the feed, the API runs SELECT … FROM posts WHERE author_id IN (SELECT followee_id FROM follows WHERE follower_id = ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Nothing is precomputed, so a new post is visible to everyone instantly, deleting a post is a single DELETE, and there is no extra infrastructure to run. With indexes on follows(follower_id) and posts(author_id, created_at) PostgreSQL answers this in milliseconds for users following a few hundred accounts. We consciously accept that the work is repeated on every feed load; at this scale CPU is cheap and correctness is free. The cost that will bite later is already visible in the query plan: the work grows with the number of followed accounts and is paid on the read path, which is the path that is 100 times busier.

nodes.label: Mobile / Web Client
nodes.why: Calls GET /feed on open and POST /posts to publish; pagination is by created_at cursor.

nodes.label: API Server
nodes.why: Stateless; the feed endpoint is a single JOIN over follows and posts ordered by time.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Three tables with two indexes serve both write and read paths; the follow graph and posts live together so one query can join them.

steps.title: Fan-out on write into Redis timelines
steps.problem: Feed loads became the database's dominant cost. Users following 2,000 accounts trigger a JOIN that scans thousands of posts and sorts them on every refresh, the same result is recomputed for every pull-to-refresh, and p99 climbed past a second under evening traffic while write load stayed trivial. Reads must stop doing the expensive work.
steps.why: Invert the cost: do the expensive work once, at write time, when a post is created, instead of on every read. When a user publishes, the API stores the post and enqueues a fan-out job; a worker looks up the author's followers and LPUSHes the post id onto each follower's timeline list in Redis, trimming each list to the newest ~800 ids. Reading the feed is now LRANGE on one key plus hydrating 20 post ids from a post cache — O(1) work regardless of how many accounts the user follows, answered in a few milliseconds. The queue between API and worker matters: publishing returns as soon as the job is accepted, and a slow fan-out delays visibility by seconds rather than delaying the poster. The costs are write amplification (a post by an account with 10,000 followers is 10,000 Redis writes), memory for a timeline per user including users who never come back (mitigated by only maintaining timelines for users active in the last N days and rebuilding others from the pull query on demand), and a new consistency wrinkle — a deleted post must be removed from many timelines, which we handle lazily by filtering deleted ids during hydration. Memory for timelines is cheap compared with the database CPU it saves, and a lost Redis can be rebuilt from PostgreSQL using the step-1 query.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Unchanged API; the feed now returns faster and a post appears in followers' feeds after a short delay.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: The API is stateless and now scales horizontally because feed reads no longer hit the database.

nodes.label: API Servers
nodes.why: GET /feed = LRANGE timeline:user + hydrate; POST /posts = INSERT then publish a fan-out job and return 202.

nodes.label: Job Queue
nodes.why: Decouples publishing from delivery; a burst of posts becomes a backlog that workers drain rather than slow API responses.

nodes.label: Fan-out Workers
nodes.why: For each job: fetch follower ids from the database, LPUSH + LTRIM each follower's timeline in Redis pipelines of thousands of commands.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.why: One list of post ids per active user capped at ~800 entries, plus a hash per post for hydration; the entire read path lives here.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Still owns users, follows and posts; now sees writes and follower lookups instead of every feed read.

steps.title: Hybrid fan-out for high-follower accounts
steps.problem: A single celebrity post now means ten million Redis writes. One such post occupies the worker fleet for minutes, every other user's posts queue behind it so 'visible within seconds' fails for everyone, and when several large accounts post during a live event the queue backlog grows faster than it drains. Pure fan-out on write does not scale with follower count.
steps.why: Combine both models based on who is posting. Accounts below a follower threshold (say 100,000) keep fan-out on write exactly as in step 2. Accounts above it are marked as 'hot' and their posts are not fanned out at all; instead each hot account keeps a short list of its recent post ids in a dedicated Redis key. At read time the feed service takes the user's precomputed timeline, looks up which hot accounts the user follows (a small cached set — nobody follows more than a few hundred celebrities), fetches their recent post ids, and merges the two sorted streams by time before hydrating. Write cost is now bounded by the threshold regardless of follower count, and read cost grows only by a handful of extra Redis lookups. The costs: the read path is no longer a single LRANGE and needs careful latency budgeting with parallel fetches, the hot-account set must be recomputed as follower counts change (an account crossing the threshold triggers a one-off backfill of its followers' timelines in the other direction), and the follow graph is consulted on the read path again — so it is moved into its own store that is cheap to read by follower id and sharded by user. This is the design most large social products converge on; the threshold is tuned by measuring worker backlog against read latency.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Unchanged.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Unchanged.

nodes.label: Feed Service
nodes.why: Reads the user's timeline, the set of hot accounts they follow and each hot account's recent posts in parallel, merges by time, then hydrates.

nodes.label: Post Service
nodes.role: Create post · route by author size
nodes.why: Stores the post; if the author is below the threshold it enqueues fan-out, otherwise it appends to the author's hot-posts list only.

nodes.label: Job Queue
nodes.why: Backlog stays bounded because no single job can exceed the threshold in size.

nodes.label: Fan-out Workers
nodes.why: Unchanged logic; now never blocked behind a celebrity post.

nodes.label: Redis: timelines
nodes.why: Same as step 2 but contains only posts from normal-sized accounts.

nodes.label: Redis: hot-account posts
nodes.why: A few hundred keys read by millions of feeds — kept replicated across several Redis replicas to spread the read load.

nodes.label: Follow Graph Store
nodes.why: Answers 'which hot accounts does user X follow' and 'who follows author Y' cheaply; split from the posts database because its access pattern and growth differ.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL: posts
nodes.why: Owns post rows and hydrates cache misses.

steps.title: Ranking service fed by Kafka engagement events
steps.problem: The feed is fast but not good. A chronological merge shows hundreds of low-value posts and buries the few a user would care about; likes, comments and dwell time are recorded in the database but never influence what is shown; and product wants a relevance-ranked feed plus metrics to evaluate it. The serving path has no notion of a score and no stream of signals to compute one from.
steps.why: Two additions. First, every user action — post, like, comment, follow, view, dwell — becomes an event on Kafka, partitioned by user id. Kafka rather than the job queue because these events have many consumers (counters, ranking features, analytics, moderation) and must be replayable to rebuild a feature store; a work queue delivers each message once to one worker and then it is gone. An aggregation consumer keeps per-post engagement counters and per-user affinity features in Redis. Second, the read path gains a ranking service: the feed service produces a candidate set (the merged chronological list from step 3, ~500 ids), the ranking service scores each candidate from cached features with a lightweight model, and the top results are returned with a small share of fresh chronological posts mixed in so new content can earn engagement. Scores are cached per user for a short TTL so refreshes within a minute are cheap. The costs are real: Kafka and a feature store are heavy infrastructure, the latency budget must now be split across candidate generation, feature fetch and scoring (mitigated by fetching features in bulk and scoring in parallel), engagement counters are eventually consistent by seconds, and ranking needs an evaluation loop (A/B tests, held-out chronological control) or it silently degrades the product while looking busy.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Sends likes, comments, views and dwell time as events alongside feed requests.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Unchanged.

nodes.label: Feed Service
nodes.why: Builds the ~500-id candidate set from timelines and hot posts (step 3) and hands it to the ranker.

nodes.label: Ranking Service
nodes.why: Fetches features for candidates in bulk from the feature store, scores them with a lightweight model, mixes in fresh posts and caches the result per user for ~60 s.

nodes.label: Post / Action API
nodes.why: Persists posts and actions, then publishes each as an event to Kafka; fan-out from step 3 is now a Kafka consumer too.

nodes.label: Kafka
nodes.why: Durable, replayable, many independent consumer groups; partitioned by user id so per-user features are computed in order.

nodes.label: Aggregation Consumers
nodes.why: Maintain per-post engagement counts and per-user affinity to authors and topics in the feature store; also drive fan-out workers from the same log.

nodes.label: Redis: features
nodes.why: Hashes per post and per user read in bulk by the ranker; values lag reality by the consumer's processing delay.

nodes.label: Redis: timelines + hot posts
nodes.why: The step-3 stores, unchanged.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Source of truth for content; the ranker never reads it on the hot path.

steps.title: Sharded storage and a CDN for media
steps.problem: Two ceilings arrived together. The posts table holds billions of rows and the single primary is out of write throughput and disk; every schema migration is a multi-day event. And media is the bandwidth: images and video uploaded through the API servers saturate their network, and a user in another continent waits seconds for a photo that lives in one region.
steps.why: Storage first. Posts are sharded by post id, where ids are time-ordered 64-bit values (timestamp plus shard plus sequence) generated by the post service, so a timeline of ids can be hydrated with point lookups routed straight to the owning shard and 'recent posts by author' stays a range scan within one shard because an author's posts are co-located by including the author in the shard key. The follow graph was already sharded by user in step 3. A wide-column or key-value store is a common alternative for the posts table because the access pattern is entirely by key; we keep PostgreSQL shards for familiarity and transactions within a shard, and note that a managed key-value store would remove the resharding operations we now own. Media second. Clients upload directly to object storage using short-lived presigned URLs, so bytes never pass through API servers; an upload event on Kafka triggers a media worker that generates thumbnails and transcodes video into adaptive bitrate renditions; and a CDN serves every rendition from edge locations with long cache lifetimes, since media objects are immutable and versioned by content hash. Redis becomes a cluster because timelines, hot posts and features no longer fit one instance. The costs are that cross-shard queries (search, global trends) now need separate pipelines fed from Kafka, resharding is an operational project that must be rehearsed, presigned uploads require an explicit 'upload complete' confirmation step to avoid orphaned objects, and transcoding is a real compute bill — justified only because bandwidth through the origin would cost more.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Fetches media from the nearest CDN edge and uploads to object storage with a presigned URL obtained from the API.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.why: Serves immutable, content-hash-addressed images and video renditions from edge locations worldwide; origin sees only cache misses.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Unchanged; now carries only JSON, not media bytes.

nodes.label: Feed + Ranking
nodes.why: Unchanged logic; hydrates post ids by routing each to its shard and returns CDN URLs for media.

nodes.label: Post / Media API
nodes.why: Generates time-ordered post ids, issues presigned upload URLs, records 'upload complete' and publishes events.

nodes.label: Object Storage
nodes.why: Receives uploads directly from clients and is the CDN origin; effectively unlimited, durable and cheap per GB.

nodes.label: Redis Cluster
nodes.why: Clustered so the hot set is partitioned across nodes; each key type keeps the semantics from earlier steps.

nodes.label: Kafka
nodes.why: Same log as step 4; an 'upload complete' event now also triggers transcoding.

nodes.label: Media Workers
nodes.why: Consume upload events, produce renditions into object storage and mark the post's media as ready; retried on failure.

nodes.label: Posts Shard 1
nodes.why: Time-ordered ids with an embedded shard component route hydration lookups without a directory service.

nodes.label: Posts Shard N
nodes.why: Adding a shard adds write throughput and disk; each shard has its own replicas for reads and failover.

textAlternative: Five diagrams show a news feed growing. Step 1: a client calls one API server that runs a single SQL query joining follows and posts in PostgreSQL. Step 2: publishing a post enqueues a fan-out job; workers push the post id onto each follower's Redis timeline list, and the feed is read from Redis instead of the database. Step 3: accounts with huge follower counts are not fanned out; a feed service merges the user's precomputed timeline with recent posts of followed hot accounts at read time, and the follow graph moves to its own sharded store. Step 4: every user action is published to Kafka; aggregation consumers maintain engagement features in Redis, and a ranking service scores candidates before the feed is returned. Step 5: posts are sharded across PostgreSQL shards by time-ordered id, Redis becomes a cluster, clients upload media directly to object storage with presigned URLs, media workers transcode via Kafka events, and a CDN serves all media from the edge.
